growth_story.headline: South Sudan's income per person fell by more than half after the 2012 oil shutdown and civil war, and oil still drives its sharpest swings.
growth_story.arc: South Sudan's record of income per person is short, running only from 2008 to 2015, too few years for the tool to mark separate eras. Income per person barely moved in 2009 and 2010, peaked in 2010, slipped 9.7 percent in 2011, the year of independence, and then fell 48.4 percent in 2012, when the government shut down oil production. It recovered 9.0 percent in 2013 and 2.7 percent in 2014, but civil war, which began in 2013, and a fall in oil prices and production in 2014 were followed by a drop of 9.8 percent in 2015. By 2015, the last year in the data, income per person was 52.9 percent below its 2010 peak and below its 2008 level, and growth averaged -8.0 percent a year over the seven years recorded. The sources link this record to heavy reliance on oil for exports and government revenue, and to overlapping crises since independence that held back institutions, infrastructure and skills.

threads.title: Oil shutdown after independence
threads.text: South Sudan became independent in 2011, and in 2012 the government shut down oil production. The IMF records that foreign exchange earnings fell then and again in 2014, when oil prices and output dropped. In the data, income per person fell 48.4 percent in 2012.

citations.quote: foreign exchange receipts fell; first during the 2012 government’s shutdown of oil production and then again when oil prices and production fell in 2014

threads.title: Civil war, 2013 to 2018
threads.text: Civil war broke out in 2013 and lasted until 2018, driving many people from their homes. The World Bank says overlapping crises since independence have held back basic institutions, infrastructure and skills.

citations.title: Republic of South Sudan: 2023 Article IV Consultation, and First and Second Reviews under the Staff-Monitored Program with Board Involvement (Country Report No. 24/160)

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: South Sudan

threads.title: Sudan's war cuts the pipeline
threads.text: All of South Sudan's oil reaches world markets through a pipeline across Sudan. Fighting in Sudan damaged it, and from February 2024 exports fell sharply until the pipeline reopened in early 2025.

citations.title: Republic of South Sudan: 2023 Article IV Consultation, and First and Second Reviews under the Staff-Monitored Program with Board Involvement (Country Report No. 24/160)
citations.quote: The conflict in Sudan has compromised the oil pipeline to Port Sudan––which carries all of South Sudan’s oil to international markets.

citations.title: Republic of South Sudan: 2023 Article IV Consultation, and First and Second Reviews under the Staff-Monitored Program with Board Involvement (Country Report No. 24/160)
citations.quote: As a result of damages to the pipeline, oil exports have since mid-February 2024 declined to about one-third of their previous level.

threads.title: Oil wealth, weak institutions
threads.text: Oil provides almost all exports and most government revenue, so the economy rises and falls with the oil flow. The World Bank says weak institutions and poor governance have kept oil money from turning into investment, public services or savings.

citations.title: Republic of South Sudan: 2023 Article IV Consultation, and First and Second Reviews under the Staff-Monitored Program with Board Involvement (Country Report No. 24/160)
citations.quote: given that oil exports account for nearly 90 percent of fiscal revenues and 95 percent of exports

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: South Sudan
citations.quote: Weak institutions, poor governance, and limited accountability have prevented oil wealth from translating into productive investment, better public services, or fiscal buffers

threads.title: Printed money, falling currency
threads.text: The central bank has repeatedly financed government spending by creating money. The IMF ties this to the currency's fall since the civil war ended, and the World Bank calls it the main source of pressure on the exchange rate and of inflation.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: South Sudan
citations.quote: Monetary financing of on- and off-budget spending remains the main source of macroeconomic instability, fueling exchange-rate pressures and inflation.

citations.title: Republic of South Sudan: 2023 Article IV Consultation, and First and Second Reviews under the Staff-Monitored Program with Board Involvement (Country Report No. 24/160)
citations.quote: Periodic monetary financing has been a major contributor to the depreciation of the SSP since the formal end of South Sudan’s civil war.

since_last_year.text: Oil production resumed in 2025 after the pipeline through Sudan reopened. The World Bank estimates a large one-off rebound in output in the 2026 fiscal year, and it expects growth to slow again in 2027 and 2028 as the rebound fades.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: South Sudan
citations.quote: Growth is projected to slow in 2027 and 2028 after the one-off oil production rebound

citations.title: IMF and South Sudan Reach Staff-Level Agreement on a Nine-Month Staff-Monitored Program
citations.quote: oil production has resumed from the oil pipeline damaged in February 2024

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a strong oil-led rebound in 2026, but the data record of income per person stops in 2015, so it cannot show the later war years, the pipeline shutdown or the rebound. The World Bank also expects most people to stay in extreme poverty despite the rebound, because oil creates few jobs.
